doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Lyrics and being in the moment
title: Being in the moment versus regurgitation, and Monk
summary: Gates defines being in the moment as not repeating the same show each set, with Monk's remark about waiting for them to play it right.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Can you expand on that a little bit? Because I’ve heard other people say, Herbie Hancock said, “We’re in the moment when we play.” I’m not sure what that means to everybody.
If I hear a so-called jazz performance. If I know the bass player. I know the bass player so I go to a set and I hear a rhythm section, a horn player and a singer. And they do the first

set. And then the club empties out. But I know the bass player. So I’m going to hang on the break. So I hang around for the second set. And if they do the exact same thing on the second set as they do on the first set they’re not in the moment. It’s regurgitation. It’s a job. It’s running a drill press. You might as well get a job running a drill press. The benefits are better. But there’s nothing — I don’t want to say artistic because I don’t like that word — there’s nothing spontaneous. There’s nothing that I’m moved by that makes me do something different. I mean I have seen some really high end professional people do that. And maybe they know what works. We have a show. We’ve worked out a show. We’re going to take this show on the road and we’re going to do it for nine months. Whew. I couldn’t do that. I’d be bored stiff. I would be bored stiff. I’m going to go back to Thelonious Monk because he’s one of my favorites. I saw a lot of concerts of Monk on YouTube. I got some live recordings of his, I’ve got records of his. Somebody interviewed him a very long time ago and said, “Mr. Monk, in essence you play the same music over and over again. Why is that?” And Monk said, “I’m waiting for them to play it right.” Well I think he was half kidding, because he had some great bands. I mean that music was elevating when they played.

But that’s just me, I’m not saying that it’s wrong. If I want to play a bossa nova then I’ll play a bossa nova. And if I want to play a waltz I won’t turn “Take Five” into a waltz. I mean I heard, “Let’s play ‘Take Five’ in six.” Why? Play something in six if you want to play something in six.” But we want to be innovative.
